name: Converse headless XMPP agent coordination daemon
description: This project explores XMPP as a coordination layer for multiple LLM coding agents. A Converse XMPP client runs as a headless NodeJS daemon with a CLI that agents call to join a password-restricted, members-only MUC groupchat shared with the other agents in a workspace and the user. Agents announce tasks and status updates in the MUC, hand off sidequests and tangential requirements that arise mid-session to idle parallel agents, and coordinate work such as rebasing and fixing conflicts when another agent's PR is merged. Tasks can be assigned via XMPP DMs, groupchat, or Claude Code, and a /coordination Claude Code skill (enabled by default via a hook) ensures the daemon is running and joins each new agent to the MUC. Planned extensions include PubSub with a web UI of vertical swimlanes showing which agents are active, what they are working on, and for how long. The tools are designed to be harness- and inference-provider-neutral.
problem: Multiple LLM agents running in parallel work in isolation; the goal is to let them collaborate more efficiently, stay aware of each other's progress, and hand off tangential sidequests that arise during sessions.

name: Hale
description: An abstract distributed systems programming language that offers fine-grained control over resources while requiring programmers to agree with the compiler on resource intent. description: Tuppence is an online payment platform ('payment rails') for businesses, developers and agents. Roadmap includes ticketing and a 'treasury' feature with 4% yield on earnings, FDIC/FSCS insurance, multi-currency fiat balances (USD, EUR, GBP) and stablecoin balances (OUSD, USDC), and bank account numbers for sending and receiving funds. name: Bonsai
description: A voxel game engine in development for ~10 years that represents worlds as collections of SDFs (density fields). The world generator and editor run almost entirely on the GPU via a three-stage pipeline: a user-configurable GLSL 'shaping' shader, a fused stage that computes normals, runs a user-configurable 'decoration' function and applies SDF edits compiled from a graph structure into bytecode, and a final convolution/packing stage producing 32-bit occupancy, color, and normal per voxel. The entire pipeline is a single fused 'ubershader' dispatched three times to keep driver overhead near zero. GPU results are passed back to the CPU for entity/structure spawning callbacks, then meshed with a fast binary meshing algorithm; surface chunks store 16 bits per voxel (1 occupancy bit, 15 normal bits) and scale to worlds larger than 1B voxels cubed. Profiling shows ~500B-1T perlin samples per second on a 3080ti mobile, with headroom from 16/8-bit textures. Designed to give users easy-to-use tools plus granular control over final output.

name: Reversible incremental sorting algorithm
description: A sorting algorithm for scenarios where the cost of comparisons is high and heterogeneous, intended as a methodology for minimizing the number of pairwise human evaluations (e.g., in AI, marketing, search evaluation, and clinical trials). It tracks which pairs are solidly established, which parts of the ranking remain ambiguous, and which alternatives are still possible/impactful, deducing the fraction of the sorting that can be reused during updates — reversible incremental ranking with information-theoretic guarantees and updates that scale linearly with the number of items. It also has a machine learning application as differentiable sorting and ranking, with reported performance of 27ms and 0.18MB for sorting 8,000 items versus 1.9s and 488MB for softsort, and about 100ms and 15MB for 10^6 items, running in O(n log n) time and O(n) space like fastsoftsort while allowing linear-time ranking updates on subsequent runs.

name: Distributed operating system for ML resources
description: A distributed operating system for managing machine learning resources, coordinating the entire memory hierarchy, networking, and compute hierarchy. The project explores upcycling end-of-life NVIDIA GPUs (K80, M40, P100), offloading MoE expert calculations to MCUs with NPUs and possibly FPGAs, and managing a 10G LAN-attached network of older Xeon servers with GPUs and USB-attached MCUs as a machine learning fabric. It also investigates bypassing end-of-life CUDA driver support for older NVIDIA hardware using Rust/Vulkan and applying ideas from IBM's ACP/TPF operating system and Workload Manager, plus architectures like Freetoken (MoE caching/routing, Engram, KV-cache compression) and other efficient-modeling approaches.

name: vision3d
description: An open-source library that extends the torchvision API to 3D object detection tasks. It provides semantic tensor types (point clouds, images, bounding boxes) built on torchvision's TVTensor, transforms that verify geometric consistency when composed, dataloaders, 3D object detection metrics, and optional visualization utilities, aiming for interoperability with torchvision image transforms. Under the hood it uses the Torch Stable ABI for custom CUDA/C++ extensions so a single wheel works across PyTorch >= 2.10, and statically links the CUDA runtime so it works out of the box on hosts with CUDA >= 12.8. Work is underway to support static tensor shape type checking via Pyrefly.
problem: Existing 3D object detection frameworks like mmdetection3d and OpenPCDet try to do too much beyond what is needed for a good 3D ML library.

description: An in-process, peer-to-peer, event-sourced categorical database written in Rust. name: Cellaflow
description: Cellaflow is a runtime that makes retries safe for AI agent tool calls by focusing on side effects rather than just agent state: it tracks which agent is allowed to perform an operation, what has already been done, and how to recover safely when an agent crashes or disappears mid-execution. It sits underneath existing agent frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, or custom agent code) without requiring the agent itself to be migrated.
problem: Recovering an agent's state after a crash is the easy half, but recovering after the agent has already performed an irreversible operation is hard. Without idempotent downstream APIs, retries can repeat side effects like sending emails, creating tickets, triggering webhooks, provisioning resources, or mutating another system.
audience: Talks to people running AI agents in production who have hit duplicate tool calls, duplicate side effects, or workflows that quietly never finished.

name: Loa
description: This app is an open source coding agent named Loa designed to run against self-hosted LLM environments such as Ollama, targeting non-cloud-sized models (e.g. a 27b model). It decomposes tasks into very simple single steps that smaller models can solve, dynamically mutates and restructures its execution plan as new context arrives, and maintains a layered memory/context system combining chat history, step results, an action backlog, reasoning explanations, and a working memory of facts and decisions. It provides a full observability UI showing memory contents, composed context, plan dependencies, artifacts, and an audit log of all executed actions, accepts mid-execution steering messages that can alter or mutate the plan, and includes error-correction and self-reflection logic (e.g. JSON repair fallbacks and hypothesis-driven retries or plan changes). It deliberately trades execution time (many inferences) for reasoning and result quality, aiming to be a hands-off agent that is briefed once and completes the task without constant reprompting, and can also serve as an analysis and discussion partner. A stable beta is planned for release.
problem: Existing coding agents target cloud-sized models and try to solve whole tasks in a handful of inferences, overloading the model and often requiring users to reprompt repeatedly until something is correctly solved; smaller self-hosted models struggle with monolithic multi-step tasks.
audience: Developers who want a hands-off coding agent running on self-hosted models

name: The Mandating Honeypots Project
description: This project demonstrates that age-verification via the Linux D-Bus interface can be trivially defeated: a simple Python script anyone can copy and paste makes the D-Bus interface always report 18+, rendering such checks useless. It argues the only reason to want ID verification is as a surveillance honeypot, and proposes a heavily redundant password-protected tool parents could use to keep kids from tampering with the verification service. Planned follow-ups include a mobile device version, an ID-database-focused version, and possibly a Windows version once the 'GetUserAgeRangeAsync' API ships.

name: SpecPilot
description: SpecPilot is a spec-driven development layer that sits in front of AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, and others. It deliberately doesn't generate code itself; instead it scaffolds a .specs/ folder and hands spec writing off to whichever agent is already in use, so specs become the artifact the agent is held to rather than a prompt retyped every session. It began as an open-source TypeScript CLI and was later given a guided chat front door of 27 questions that runs fully offline in the browser, outputting the .specs/ tree plus an IDE onboarding prompt. A recently shipped MCP server (published to the official MCP registry and Smithery) lets the agent run the questionnaire itself, and planned brownfield support would point the tool at an existing repo and backfill specs from the code. The tool is free, open source, and has no login; the author sees spec enforcement — checking diffs against specs and failing loudly — as where the lasting value lies.
problem: Coding agents only write better code when they have something firmer than a chat prompt to work against; prompts get retyped every session, and spec generation alone is easy to copy while spec enforcement is where the value is.
audience: Developers using AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot

Top engine moves are often lines that no one below master level actually plays, and existing tools don't show which moves players at or below a given rating realistically choose from a position. It tracks vehicle repair tasks, provides easy access to VIN info for parts search and DMV records, and generates in-depth diagnostic reports: a code database includes manufacturer-specific DTCs for 10 major makes plus per-model data down to the generation level (known failure patterns, common codes per engine), with AI reports conditioned on the exact year/make/model/engine. Repair price calculations mix fetched parts price data with a guided prompt using published labor-hour records and regional averages. It speaks generic OBD2 (ELM327) over Bluetooth, so cheap adapters work.
problem: The builder wanted a single tool to track vehicle tasks, easily access VIN info for parts search, and DMV records, and saw nothing on the market with comparable depth of diagnostic reporting.
audience: Car, motorcycle, tractor, and truck owners doing their own vehicle diagnostics and repairs

description: Independent lab testing service for everyday food products, screening for plastic chemicals (phthalates and bisphenols) and publishing all results publicly. It features 'Duckies' with distinct personalities (skills) that each specialize in a particular kind of problem, 'teachable moments' bubbles that surface novel, tangential, or foundational information while you work, and skill-level detection with a routing model so it doesn't overwhelm users with unneeded explanations. Each duck runs on a tiered memory model rather than a flat context window: core memory defining its skills, long-term memory for company standards and code style, a separate project-scoped long-term memory, and short-term memory for the current task, so ducks reason like team members with real employment history rather than chatbots.
problem: Juniors and new hires often fall into an impostor-syndrome trap when reading an unfamiliar codebase or reviewing a senior peer's PR; documentation usually runs into the curse of knowledge, written by people who have lost sight of what it's like to be new to the codebase.
